Predicting Match Outcomes in VCT 2026 Professional Valorant

PSTAT 131 Final Project

Ethan Anghelache

June 10, 2026

Introduction

(run at end: quarto render VCTMatch_Prediction.ipynb –to html -M code-fold:true -M toc:true -M toc-location:left -M self-contained:true)

The purpose of this project is to develop a model that will predict the win-rate outcome for upcoming valorant esports matches.

What Is Valorant?

Valorant is a team-based tactical first-person shooter developed by Riot Games, where two teams of five players compete across multiple maps to win rounds by eliminating opponents or completing objectives (planting/defusing a spike). Professional Valorant is organized through Riot’s VCT (Valorant Champions Tour) system, which consists of regional leagues (Americas, EMEA, Pacific, China) and their international events. 12 esports teams in each of the regions play such regionals to qualify for an international stage in both best of 3 and best of 5 structured games.

What Are We Trying To Do?

The goal of this project is to answer the question: “Can we accurately predict the outcome of upcoming VCT matches? More specifically, which team will win based on team and player performance statistics?” It seems quite reasonable to hypothesize that a match’s outcome would vary depending on individual performance metrics like Average Combat Score (ACS), kill-death ratio (KD), first kill rate, and clutch success rate, as well as team-level factors like recent form and map win rates. Coaching staffs and analysts in esports increasingly rely on data-driven insights to evaluate players and craft strategies, so understanding which metrics are most predictive of winning can inform roster decisions, in-game calling, and opponent scouting. So, I would like to test whether it is possible to develop a model that can predict VCT match winners based on those qualities.

This data was taken from the Kaggle dataset, “Valorant Champion Tour 2021-2026 Data”, scraped from VLR.gg by user Ryan Luong. It contains official match, player, and team statistics from VCT tournaments spanning the 2021 through 2026 competitive seasons across all tournments. In this case however, I am prioritizing only 2026 data. This includes Kickoff (first regionals of the year), and Masters Santiago (first international of the year); made up of 21 csv files that I combined myself.

The combined CSV contains 136,352 rows and 101 columns, sourced from 18+ individual files that were merged together, each contributing a different type of match data. Printing the unique _source_file values reveals how the data is distributed across sources. The largest files, kills.csv (30,675 rows) and rounds_kills.csv (26,552 rows), contain granular round and kill-level data, while smaller files like players_stats.csv (5,231 rows) and overview.csv (15,690 rows) contain the aggregated player and team-level statistics that are most relevant to our goal.

Not all 18 source files are equally useful for predicting match outcomes. Many contain granular round-level or economy-level detail that would require significant additional aggregation, or metadata files (like teams_ids.csv and tournament_stages_match_types_ids.csv) that serve only as lookup tables. For our match-level prediction task, we focus on the following key source files:

  • players_stats.csv — per-player performance stats (Rating, ACS, KD, etc.)
  • overview.csv — team-level match overview
  • maps_scores.csv — Team A/B scores per map
  • scores.csv — match-level scores
  • eco_rounds.csv — economy and round data
  • kills.csv / kills_stats.csv — kill-level data

These files collectively provide the raw material needed to engineer our match-level feature matrix in the next phase

Code

Previewing the Key Source Files

With the combined dataset split back into individual sub-dataframes, we preview the most important source files to confirm their structure before aggregating.

players_stats.csv (5,231 rows) is the most valuable file for our purposes. Each row represents a single player’s performance in a single match, containing stats including Rating, Average Combat Score (ACS), Kills, Deaths, Assists, Kill-Assist-Survive-Trade percentage (KAST%), Headshot Percentage, First Kills, First Deaths, Average Damage Per Round (ADR), and side-specific win percentages (Attacker/Defender). Since each match has 10 players (5 per team), we will aggregate these individual stats up to the team level by averaging across the 5 players on each side.

overview.csv and scores.csv contain team-level and match-level results respectively, including Team A, Team B, and the Match Result, which will serve as our target variable. maps_scores.csv provides the per-map score breakdown used to confirm match outcomes.

The output confirms that our key files are structured correctly and contain no unexpected nulls in the columns we care about. Our next step is to aggregate players_stats.csv to the team-match level, then join it with scores.csv to attach the match result as our target variable.

Aggregating Player Stats to the Team Level

Since players_stats.csv is recorded at the player level (one row per player per match), we need to aggregate it up to the team level before we can join it with match outcomes.

Code 
# Isolate Player Stats for EDA
ps = dfs['players_stats.csv'].copy()

# Clean Percentage Columns -> Numeric
pct_cols = ['Kill, Assist, Trade, Survive %', 'Headshot %',
            'Clutch Success %']
for col in pct_cols:
    ps[col] = ps[col].astype(str).str.replace('%', '').str.strip()
    ps[col] = pd.to_numeric(ps[col], errors='coerce')

# Aggregate Stats per Team per Match
numeric_features = ['Rating', 'Average Combat Score', 'Kills', 'Deaths',
                    'Assists', 'Kill, Assist, Trade, Survive %',
                    'Average Damage Per Round', 'Headshot %',
                    'First Kills', 'First Deaths', 'Kills Per Round',
                    'Assists Per Round', 'First Kills Per Round',
                    'First Deaths Per Round', 'Clutch Success %']

team_match_stats = (
    ps.groupby(['Tournament', 'Stage', 'Match Type', 'Teams'])[numeric_features]
    .mean()
    .reset_index()
)

print("Team-match aggregated stats shape:", team_match_stats.shape)
print(team_match_stats.head())

# Isolate match results (target variable)
scores = dfs['scores.csv'].copy()
non_null_scores = scores.columns[scores.notna().any()].tolist()
print("\nscores.csv non-null columns:", non_null_scores)
print(scores[non_null_scores].head(10))

We group by Tournament, Stage, Match Type, and Teams, then take the mean across all 5 players for each numeric performance stat. Percentage columns like KAST% and Headshot% are first cleaned by stripping the % symbol and converting to numeric before aggregating. The resulting team_match_stats dataframe has 349 rows and 19 columns, one row per team per match, with clean numeric averages for all key performance metrics including Rating, ACS, KD, ADR, KAST%, First Kills, and First Deaths Per Round. This is the core feature table we will use to build our final match-level dataset.

Inspecting the Target Variable

The scores.csv file contains the match-level results we need. Each row represents a single match and includes the team names (Team A and Team B), their respective scores, and a Match Result column formatted as a string — for example, “G2 Esports won”. Since our target variable needs to be numeric for modeling, we will extract the winning team name from this string and compare it against the Team A column to engineer a binary label: 1 if Team A won, 0 if Team B won. The team name columns in scores.csv also align with the Teams column in players_stats.csv, which confirms that we can join these two tables cleanly in the next step.

Building the Final Match Dataset

With both the scores and player stats aggregated, we can now construct the final match-level feature matrix. This involves three steps: cleaning the scores table down to one row per match, engineering the binary target variable, and joining Team A and Team B performance stats onto each match row.

Code 
# Clean scores to one row per match
scores_clean = dfs['scores.csv'].copy()
non_null = scores_clean.columns[scores_clean.notna().any()].tolist()
scores_clean = scores_clean[non_null].drop_duplicates(
    subset=['Tournament', 'Stage', 'Match Type', 'Match Name']
).reset_index(drop=True)

print("Unique matches:", len(scores_clean))
print(scores_clean[['Match Name', 'Team A', 'Team B', 
                      'Team A Score', 'Team B Score', 
                      'Match Result']].head(10)) 

#Create binary target — 1 if Team A won, 0 if Team B won 
scores_clean['target'] = scores_clean.apply(
    lambda row: 1 if str(row['Match Result']).strip()
                     .lower()
                     .startswith(str(row['Team A']).strip().lower())
    else 0, axis=1
)

print("\nTarget distribution:")
print(scores_clean['target'].value_counts())
print(f"\nTeam A win rate: {scores_clean['target'].mean():.2%}")

First, we deduplicate scores.csv to ensure exactly one row per unique match by dropping duplicates on Tournament, Stage, Match Type, and Match Name. This gives us 144 unique matches. We then create the binary target column using the Match Result string. If the result starts with Team A’s name, the label is 1 (Team A won), otherwise 0 (Team B won).

Next, we join the team-level aggregated stats onto the match table twice; once for Team A and once for Team B.

Code 
# Join team A stats
# Rename aggregated stats columns with team_a_ prefix
team_a_stats = team_match_stats.rename(columns={
    'Teams': 'Team A',
    **{col: f'team_a_{col}' for col in numeric_features}
})

# Rename aggregated stats columns with team_b_ prefix
team_b_stats = team_match_stats.rename(columns={
    'Teams': 'Team B',
    **{col: f'team_b_{col}' for col in numeric_features}
})

# Merge Team A stats
match_df = scores_clean.merge(
    team_a_stats[['Tournament', 'Stage', 'Match Type', 'Team A'] + 
                  [f'team_a_{c}' for c in numeric_features]],
    on=['Tournament', 'Stage', 'Match Type', 'Team A'],
    how='left'
)

# Merge Team B stats
match_df = match_df.merge(
    team_b_stats[['Tournament', 'Stage', 'Match Type', 'Team B'] + 
                  [f'team_b_{c}' for c in numeric_features]],
    on=['Tournament', 'Stage', 'Match Type', 'Team B'],
    how='left'
)

print("\nFinal match dataset shape:", match_df.shape)
print("\nMissing values per column:")
print(match_df.isnull().sum()[match_df.isnull().sum() > 0])
print("\nSample rows:")
print(match_df[['Match Name', 'Team A', 'Team B', 'target',
                 'team_a_Rating', 'team_b_Rating']].head(10))

Exploratory Data Analysis

With our final match-level dataset constructed, we now explore the data visually to understand the distribution of our target variable, identify relationships between features and match outcomes, and detect any data quality issues before modeling. The plots and analyses below inform several key preprocessing and modeling decisions made in later sections.

Missing Data

Before modeling, we must identify and address any missing values in the feature matrix. Missing data can cause errors during model training and introduce bias into predictions if not handled appropriately.

Code 
# Overall missing data summary 
total_missing = match_df.isnull().sum()
pct_missing = (match_df.isnull().sum() / len(match_df) * 100).round(2)

missing_df = pd.DataFrame({
    'Missing Count': total_missing,
    'Missing %': pct_missing
}).query('`Missing Count` > 0').sort_values('Missing %', ascending=False)

print("Missing Data Summary:")
print(missing_df)
print(f"\nTotal rows: {len(match_df)}")
print(f"Total columns with missing data: {len(missing_df)}")

# Impute missing values 
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer

# Separate feature columns
team_a_cols = [f'team_a_{c}' for c in numeric_features]
team_b_cols = [f'team_b_{c}' for c in numeric_features]
all_feature_cols = team_a_cols + team_b_cols

# Impute with median (robust to outliers)
imputer = SimpleImputer(strategy='median')
match_df[all_feature_cols] = imputer.fit_transform(match_df[all_feature_cols])

# Verify no missing values remain
print("Missing values after imputation:")
print(match_df[all_feature_cols].isnull().sum().sum())
print(f"Final shape: {match_df.shape}")

The missing data summary reveals two patterns. Clutch Success % has the most missingness for both teams (~22–23%, or 33 rows), which is expected. Clutch situations are rare events and many matches simply had no qualifying clutch rounds to record. All remaining affected columns show exactly 5 missing values (3.47%), likely corresponding to the same small set of matches with incomplete player stat data.

Since missingness is low across all columns, we impute using the column median via scikit-learn’s SimpleImputer. Median imputation is preferred over mean imputation because it is more robust to outliers. This is particularly important for a stat like Clutch Success %, which can be skewed by rare standout performances. After imputation, the missing value count drops to 0 and the dataset retains its full shape of (144, 41), confirming our feature matrix is clean and ready for exploratory analysis.

Visual EDA

Now, we will explore the relationships between select variables with the outcome as well as with eachother!

Match Outcome Between Teams

We begin by examining the distribution of our target variable: which team won! That is, across all 144 matches in the dataset. Understanding class balance is a critical first step, as a significant imbalance between outcomes can bias a model toward always predicting the majority class.

Code 
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))

# Plot 1: Count of wins 
outcome_counts = match_df['target'].value_counts()
outcome_labels = ['Team B Won (0)', 'Team A Won (1)']

            edgecolor='black', linewidth=0.8)

# Plot 2: Percentage pie chart 
axes[1].pie(outcome_counts.values, labels=outcome_labels, colors=colors,
            autopct='%1.1f%%', startangle=90,
            wedgeprops={'edgecolor': 'black', 'linewidth': 0.8})

plt.savefig('eda_plot1_outcome_distribution.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

Out of 144 total matches, 87 were won by Team B (0) and 57 were won by Team A (1), resulting in a class split of approximately 60.4% vs. 39.6%. This tells us that our dataset is moderately imbalanced. Team B wins occur notably more often than Team A wins. This is important to acknowledge before modeling because a naive classifier that always predicts “Team B wins” would achieve ~60% accuracy without learning anything meaningful. To account for this, we use stratified sampling when splitting the data into training and testing sets, ensuring that both splits reflect this 60/40 ratio and that our model is evaluated fairly across both classes.

The boxplots above compare two key player performance metrics — Rating and Average Combat Score (ACS) — between winning and losing teams across all matches in our dataset.

For Rating, winning teams show a median of approximately 1.08 compared to 0.92 for losing teams. The boxes barely overlap, indicating a clear and consistent separation between the two groups, making Rating one of the strongest individual predictors in our dataset. A few outliers exist! Teams that won despite low ratings or lost despite high ratings — but this is expected at the professional level, where team coordination and strategy can occasionally override raw individual performance.

For ACS, winning teams show a median of approximately 205 compared to 185 for losing teams (gap of roughly 20 points). There is slightly more overlap compared to Rating, but the separation remains meaningful. One notable outlier is a losing team with an ACS near 263, suggesting a team that dominated statistically on an individual level but still lost. This is likely due to factors such as economy management or team coordination that individual combat stats alone cannot capture.

Together, both Rating and ACS show statistically meaningful separation between winners and losers, providing strong justification for using these as predictors in our classification models.

Correlation Heatmap of Differential Features

Before modeling, we engineer differential features by subtracting each Team B stat from the corresponding Team A stat for every match. This transforms the problem from comparing two separate team rows into a single row of signed differences, a positive value means Team A outperformed Team B on that stat, and a negative value means the opposite. We then compute the full pairwise correlation matrix to identify which differentials are most predictive of match outcome and which features are redundant with each other.

Code 
# We compute the DIFFERENCE (Team A - Team B) for each stat.

diff_df = pd.DataFrame()

for col in numeric_features:
    diff_df[f'diff_{col}'] = match_df[f'team_a_{col}'] - match_df[f'team_b_{col}']

diff_df['target'] = match_df['target']

# Rename columns for cleaner plot labels
rename_map = {
    'diff_Rating': 'Rating Diff',
    'diff_Average Combat Score': 'ACS Diff',
    'diff_Kills': 'Kills Diff',
    'diff_Deaths': 'Deaths Diff',
    'diff_Assists': 'Assists Diff',
    'diff_Kill, Assist, Trade, Survive %': 'KAST Diff',
    'diff_Average Damage Per Round': 'ADR Diff',
    'diff_Headshot %': 'HS% Diff',
    'diff_First Kills': 'FK Diff',
    'diff_First Deaths': 'FD Diff',
    'diff_Kills Per Round': 'KPR Diff',
    'diff_Assists Per Round': 'APR Diff',
    'diff_First Kills Per Round': 'FKPR Diff',
    'diff_First Deaths Per Round': 'FDPR Diff',
    'diff_Clutch Success %': 'Clutch% Diff',
    'target': 'Match Result'
}
diff_df = diff_df.rename(columns=rename_map)

print("Differential feature matrix shape:", diff_df.shape)
print(diff_df.head(3))

# Plot correlation heatmap 
corr_matrix = diff_df.corr()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 12))

mask = np.zeros_like(corr_matrix, dtype=bool)
mask[np.triu_indices_from(mask)] = True  # mask upper triangle

sns.heatmap(
    corr_matrix,
    mask=mask,
    annot=True,
    fmt='.2f',
    cmap='RdYlGn',
    center=0,
    vmin=-1, vmax=1,
    linewidths=0.5,
    linecolor='white',
    annot_kws={'size': 8},
    ax=ax,
    square=True,
    cbar_kws={'shrink': 0.8, 'label': 'Correlation Coefficient'}
)

ax.set_title('Correlation Matrix: Team Stat Differentials vs Match Result',
             fontsize=14, fontweight='bold', pad=20)
ax.tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45, labelsize=9)
ax.tick_params(axis='y', rotation=0, labelsize=9)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('eda_plot3_correlation_heatmap.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

The heatmap reveals two critical findings for modeling.

Looking at the bottom row (correlations with Match Result), three differentials emerge as the strongest predictors: Rating Diff (0.62), KPR Diff (0.61), and ACS Diff (0.60) are nearly tied at the top, followed closely by Kills Diff (0.60), ADR Diff (0.59), and KAST Diff (0.58). FDPR Diff shows a negative correlation of -0.41, confirming that teams with more first deaths per round relative to their opponent tend to lose. Notably, HS% Diff has virtually zero correlation (-0.02) with match outcome. So individual mechanical precision matters far less than sustained combat output across the full match.

The heatmap also exposes severe multicollinearity among predictors. Rating and ADR share a correlation of 0.94, KPR and ACS share 0.99, and FKPR/FDPR cluster tightly together at 0.90. Including all of these redundant features in a standard model would inflate coefficient variance and reduce interpretability. This directly motivates our use of regularization-based models (particularly Elastic Net) which automatically shrink and select among correlated predictors in the next phase.

Key Differential Features

To complement the heatmap, we visualize two pairs of differential features directly against match outcome using scatter plots. This lets us see not just the strength of individual correlations, but how cleanly the two classes separate across two dimensions simultaneously.

             fontsize=15, fontweight='bold', y=1.02)

plt.savefig('eda_plot4_scatter_differentials.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

The left plot (First Kills vs. First Deaths Differential) shows broad scatter across all four quadrants with significant mixing of green and red dots. This confirms the heatmap finding that first contact advantages (FK and FD differentials) are moderate but not dominant predictors (~0.38 and -0.35). There is no clean diagonal boundary separating winners from losers, reflecting the reality that professional VCT teams are disciplined enough to recover from early round disadvantages through utility, economy management, and coordinated retakes.

The right plot (KPR vs. ADR Differential) tells a dramatically different story. Green dots cluster tightly in the top-right quadrant and red dots dominate the bottom-left, forming a near-perfect diagonal separation between winners and losers. There is very little color mixing near the center zero line, visually confirming that KPR and ADR differentials are among the strongest predictors in our dataset, consistent with their 0.61 and 0.59 correlations from the heatmap. Teams that simultaneously out-kill and out-damage their opponents per round win at a very high rate in VCT competition.

Together, these two plots reinforce a key narrative: sustained combat output across an entire match is a far more reliable indicator of winning than isolated first-contact advantages at the start of individual rounds.

Team A Win Rate by Tournament Stage

Our final EDA plot examines whether Team A’s win rate varies meaningfully across different tournaments and stages. Since our dataset pools matches from four regional Kickoff events and two stages of Masters Santiago, it is worth checking whether the Team A label carries any systematic bias depending on tournament context. This could influence how our model generalizes.

Code 
# Compute Team A win rate by Stage

    ['sum', 'count']
).reset_index()
stage_wins.columns = ['Tournament', 'Stage', 'Team A Wins', 'Total Matches']

The results vary considerably across the six tournament groups. The VCT China Kickoff Main Event is the only stage where Team A won more than half of all matches, at 56.7% across 30 matches. Every other stage falls at or below the 50% baseline. Americas, EMEA, and Pacific Kickoff Main Events all show Team A win rates between 30–33.3%, and the Masters Santiago Swiss Stage sits at 40.0%. The Masters Santiago Playoffs group is the only other near-balanced group at exactly 50.0%, though its sample size of only 14 matches makes it the least reliable estimate.

This variation confirms that the Team A label is not uniformly assigned across tournaments. Win rates differ systematically by region and stage. The overall 60/40 class imbalance observed earlier is partially explained by how Team A and Team B were designated in lower win-rate stages like EMEA and Pacific. Importantly, this also tells us that tournament or stage identity alone is not a reliable predictor of match outcome, reinforcing our decision to build the model entirely around performance differential features rather than metadata.

This concludes our exploratory analysis. The five plots above collectively establish that KPR, Rating, and ACS differentials are the strongest predictors of match outcome, that multicollinearity among features is significant and must be addressed through regularization, and that our dataset is moderately imbalanced in a way that requires stratified sampling during model training.

Setting up for the Models

Feature Matrix Definition

With EDA complete, we now prepare the data for modeling. Our feature matrix X consists entirely of the 15 differential features engineered earlier. One signed difference (Team A minus Team B) for each performance stat. We deliberately exclude raw team_a_ and team_b_ columns from the model, as the differential representation is more informative: a positive value directly indicates Team A outperformed Team B on that stat, making the signal cleaner and more interpretable for a binary classifier.

The target vector y is the binary Match Result column (1 = Team A won, 0 = Team B won). The confirmed shapes — X: (144, 15) and y: (144,) verify that our feature matrix and target are correctly aligned before splitting.

Code 
# Define feature matrix and target 

feature_cols = [col for col in diff_df.columns if col != 'Match Result']
X = diff_df[feature_cols]
y = diff_df['Match Result']

print("Feature matrix shape:", X.shape)
print("Target shape:", y.shape)
print("\nFeature columns:")
print(feature_cols)
Feature matrix shape: (144, 15)
Target shape: (144,)

Feature columns:
['Rating Diff', 'ACS Diff', 'Kills Diff', 'Deaths Diff', 'Assists Diff', 'KAST Diff', 'ADR Diff', 'HS% Diff', 'FK Diff', 'FD Diff', 'KPR Diff', 'APR Diff', 'FKPR Diff', 'FDPR Diff', 'Clutch% Diff']

Data Split

We split the dataset into a 70% training set (100 matches) and a 30% test set (44 matches) using train_test_split with stratify=y. Stratified sampling ensures that both splits reflect the same class proportions as the full dataset. Thjis is critical here because our target is moderately imbalanced at ~60/40. Without stratification, random chance could produce a training set that over-represents one class, causing the model to learn a biased decision boundary.

A fixed random_state=131 is used to ensure full reproducibility of all results.

Code 
# Stratified Train/Test Split (70/30) 
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y,
    test_size=0.30,
    random_state=131,       
    stratify=y              # stratify on outcome 
)

print("Training set size:", X_train.shape)
print("Testing set size: ", X_test.shape)

print("\nTraining target distribution:")
print(y_train.value_counts())
print(f"Training Team A win rate: {y_train.mean():.2%}")

print("\nTesting target distribution:")
print(y_test.value_counts())
print(f"Testing Team A win rate:  {y_test.mean():.2%}")

# Verify stratification worked
train_pct = y_train.mean()
test_pct  = y_test.mean()
full_pct  = y.mean()

print("\nStratification Check:")
print(f"  Full dataset Team A win rate:  {full_pct:.2%}")
print(f"  Training set Team A win rate:  {train_pct:.2%}")
print(f"  Testing set  Team A win rate:  {test_pct:.2%}")
print(f"\n  ✅ Stratification successful!" 
      if abs(train_pct - test_pct) < 0.05 
      else "  ⚠️ Check stratification")

The stratification check confirms the split worked correctly. The full dataset Team A win rate of 39.58% is preserved in both the training set (40.00%) and the test set (38.64%), a difference of less than 2 percentage points across both splits. The test set is held out completely and will not be touched until final model evaluation, ensuring our reported test accuracy is a true out-of-sample estimate and not influenced by any tuning decisions made during training

K-Fold Cross Validation

All four models will be evaluated using Stratified 5-Fold Cross Validation on the training set before any final evaluation on the held-out test set. In k-fold CV, the training data is split into 5 equal folds and the model trains on 4 folds and validates on the remaining 1, rotating through all combinations. This gives us 5 independent accuracy estimates which we average to produce a reliable CV score that is far less sensitive to the luck of a single train/val split.

We use k=5 because it strikes the right balance for our dataset size of 100 training samples. Each fold uses 80 samples for training and 20 for validation, which is enough data to train meaningfully while still producing a useful validation signal. shuffle=True withrandom_state=131 ensures the fold assignments are randomized but reproducible.

Code 
# Define Stratified K-Fold Cross Validation
# k=5 is standard for datasets of this size (100 training samples)
# Stratified ensures each fold maintains the ~40/60 class ratio

skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=131)

print("Cross-Validation Configuration:")
print(f"  Method:      Stratified K-Fold")
print(f"  K (folds):   5")
print(f"  Shuffle:     True")
print(f"  Random seed: 131")

# Preview what each fold looks like 
print("\nFold-by-fold breakdown:")
print(f"{'Fold':<6} {'Train Size':<12} {'Val Size':<10} {'Train Win%':<12} {'Val Win%'}")
print("-" * 55)

for fold, (train_idx, val_idx) in enumerate(skf.split(X_train, y_train), 1):
    fold_train_y = y_train.iloc[train_idx]
    fold_val_y   = y_train.iloc[val_idx]
    print(f"{fold:<6} {len(train_idx):<12} {len(val_idx):<10} "
          f"{fold_train_y.mean():.2%}      {fold_val_y.mean():.2%}")
Cross-Validation Configuration:
  Method:      Stratified K-Fold
  K (folds):   5
  Shuffle:     True
  Random seed: 131

Fold-by-fold breakdown:
Fold   Train Size   Val Size   Train Win%   Val Win%
-------------------------------------------------------
1      80           20         40.00%      40.00%
2      80           20         40.00%      40.00%
3      80           20         40.00%      40.00%
4      80           20         40.00%      40.00%
5      80           20         40.00%      40.00%

The fold-by-fold breakdown confirms that stratification is working perfectly across all 5 folds. Every fold maintains exactly 40.00% Team A win rate in both the training portion (80 samples) and the validation portion (20 samples). Which is identical to the overall training set class ratio. This guarantees that no single fold accidentally over- or under-represents one class, and that our CV accuracy scores reflect balanced, unbiased performance estimates across all folds.

Model Building

We fit four classification models to predict VCT match outcomes from the 15 differential features. Before fitting any model, we establish a naive baseline by computing the accuracy of always predicting the majority class (Team B wins). Since Team B wins 60% of training matches, any model that cannot beat this threshold provides no predictive value over a trivial guess.

All features are already numeric continuous differentials; no categorical encoding is required. We apply StandardScaler to center each feature to mean ≈ 0 and standard deviation ≈ 1. Scaling is fit only on the training set and then applied to the test set, preventing any data leakage from test distribution into the preprocessing step. This is critical for Logistic Regression and SVM, which are sensitive to feature scale, and does not hurt the tree-based models.

Code 
# Quick baseline: what accuracy would always predicting Team B give?
baseline_acc = (y_train == 0).sum() / len(y_train)
print(f"\nBaseline accuracy (always predict Team B wins): {baseline_acc:.2%}")
print("Our models must beat this to be useful!")
print(f"\nTraining set: {X_train.shape[0]} matches")
print(f"Each fold trains on ~{int(X_train.shape[0]*0.8)} and validates on ~{int(X_train.shape[0]*0.2)} matches")

Baseline accuracy (always predict Team B wins): 60.00%
Our models must beat this to be useful!

Training set: 100 matches
Each fold trains on ~80 and validates on ~20 matches
Code 
# Build preprocessing pipeline 
# StandardScaler: centers each feature to mean=0, std=1
# Critical for Logistic Regression and SVM
# Tree-based models (RF, GBT) don't require scaling but it doesn't hurt

preprocessor = Pipeline(steps=[
    ('scaler', StandardScaler())
])

# Fit on training data only 
X_train_scaled = preprocessor.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled  = preprocessor.transform(X_test)

Fitting the Model

Each model follows the same fitting process. The steps are described once here and apply to all four models.

For each model, the following steps were carried out:

  1. Define the model — specify the classifier, any fixed settings (e.g., random_state=131, class_weight='balanced'), and the parameter grid of hyperparameter values to search over.

  2. Wrap in a search object — use GridSearchCV (or RandomizedSearchCV for large grids) with our Stratified 5-Fold CV object skf and scoring='accuracy'.

  3. Fit on scaled training data — call .fit(X_train_scaled, y_train) to simultaneously tune hyperparameters and train the model entirely within the training set. The test set is never touched at this stage.

  4. Extract best results — retrieve best_params_ and best_score_ to record the optimal hyperparameter configuration and its mean CV accuracy across all 5 folds.

The code and outputs of each is show below:

Code 
# Logistic Regression (Elastic Net) 
# Elastic net combines L1 (Lasso) + L2 (Ridge) regularization
# Great for our data since we have multicollinear features (ACS/Rating/KPR)

lr_param_grid = {
    'C': [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100],        # regularization strength
    'l1_ratio': [0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0]     # 0=Ridge, 1=Lasso, mid=ElasticNet
}

lr_model = LogisticRegression(
    penalty='elasticnet',
    solver='saga',
    max_iter=10000,
    random_state=131
)

lr_grid = GridSearchCV(
    estimator=lr_model,
    param_grid=lr_param_grid,
    cv=skf,
    scoring='accuracy',
    n_jobs=-1,
    verbose=0
)

lr_grid.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)

print("=" * 50)
print("LOGISTIC REGRESSION (Elastic Net) RESULTS")
print("=" * 50)
print(f"Best Parameters:    {lr_grid.best_params_}")
print(f"Best CV Accuracy:   {lr_grid.best_score_:.4f} ({lr_grid.best_score_*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"Baseline Accuracy:  {baseline_acc:.4f} ({baseline_acc*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"Improvement:        +{(lr_grid.best_score_ - baseline_acc)*100:.2f}%")
print()

# Random Forest
rf_param_grid = {
    'n_estimators': [100, 200, 300],        # number of trees in the forest
    'max_depth': [3, 5, 10, None],          # how deep each tree can grow
    'max_features': ['sqrt', 'log2', None], # features considered at each split
    'min_samples_split': [2, 5, 10]         # min samples needed to split a node
}

rf_model = RandomForestClassifier(
    random_state=131,
    class_weight='balanced'   # handles our 40/60 class imbalance
)

rf_grid = GridSearchCV(
    estimator=rf_model,
    param_grid=rf_param_grid,
    cv=skf,
    scoring='accuracy',
    n_jobs=-1,
    verbose=0
)

rf_grid.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)

print("=" * 50)
print("RANDOM FOREST RESULTS")
print("=" * 50)
print(f"Best Parameters:    {rf_grid.best_params_}")
print(f"Best CV Accuracy:   {rf_grid.best_score_:.4f} ({rf_grid.best_score_*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"Baseline Accuracy:  {baseline_acc:.4f} ({baseline_acc*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"Improvement:        +{(rf_grid.best_score_ - baseline_acc)*100:.2f}%"   )
print()

#Gradient Boosting Classifier 
gbt_param_grid = {
    'n_estimators': [100, 200, 300],         # number of boosting rounds
    'learning_rate': [0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2], # how much each tree contributes
    'max_depth': [2, 3, 4],                   # depth of each weak learner
    'subsample': [0.7, 0.8, 1.0]             # fraction of samples per tree
}

gbt_model = GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=131)

gbt_grid = RandomizedSearchCV(    # RandomizedSearch since grid is large (108 combos)
    estimator=gbt_model,
    param_distributions=gbt_param_grid,
    n_iter=40,                    # try 40 random combinations
    cv=skf,
    scoring='accuracy',
    n_jobs=-1,
    random_state=131,
    verbose=0
)

gbt_grid.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)

print("=" * 50)
print("GRADIENT BOOSTED TREE RESULTS")
print("=" * 50)
print(f"Best Parameters:    {gbt_grid.best_params_}")
print(f"Best CV Accuracy:   {gbt_grid.best_score_:.4f} ({gbt_grid.best_score_*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"Baseline Accuracy:  {baseline_acc:.4f} ({baseline_acc*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"Improvement:        +{(gbt_grid.best_score_ - baseline_acc)*100:.2f}%")
print()

# Support Vector Machine 
svm_param_grid = {
    'C': [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100],                    # regularization
    'kernel': ['linear', 'rbf', 'poly'],              # decision boundary shape
    'gamma': ['scale', 'auto', 0.01, 0.1]            # kernel coefficient
}

svm_model = SVC(
    random_state=131,
    probability=True,       # enables predict_proba for win probability later
    class_weight='balanced'
)

svm_grid = GridSearchCV(
    estimator=svm_model,
    param_grid=svm_param_grid,
    cv=skf,
    scoring='accuracy',
    n_jobs=-1,
    verbose=0
)

svm_grid.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)

print("=" * 50)
print("SUPPORT VECTOR MACHINE RESULTS")
print("=" * 50)
print(f"Best Parameters:    {svm_grid.best_params_}")
print(f"Best CV Accuracy:   {svm_grid.best_score_:.4f} ({svm_grid.best_score_*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"Baseline Accuracy:  {baseline_acc:.4f} ({baseline_acc*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"Improvement:        +{(svm_grid.best_score_ - baseline_acc)*100:.2f}%")

The plot reveals a clear sweet spot at C = 0.1 with the balanced Elastic Net (l1_ratio = 0.5). At very low C (0.001), pure Ridge performs reasonably at 82%, but all l1_ratio variants except pure Lasso collapse to the 60% baseline at C = 0.01, indicating that over-regularization is harmful when the penalty is L1-heavy. Accuracy stabilizes and converges across all l1_ratios as C increases, confirming that moderate regularization with a blended penalty is optimal for our multicollinear feature set.

Results of the Best Models

Both Logistic Regression and SVM tied at 84.00% CV accuracy during tuning, making a direct test-set comparison necessary to determine the final best model. We evaluate both on the 44 held-out matches using test accuracy, ROC-AUC score, and a full classification report broken down by class.

Test Set Evaluation

We pass each model’s best estimator (retrieved directly from GridSearchCV via best_estimator_) to predict on X_test_scaled. We compute both hard predictions (predict) and win probability estimates (predict_proba) for each match, storing all results for downstream visualization.

Code 
#  Evaluate top 2 models on test set 
best_models = {
    'Logistic Regression': lr_grid.best_estimator_,
    'SVM':                 svm_grid.best_estimator_
}

test_results = {}

for name, model in best_models.items():
    y_pred  = model.predict(X_test_scaled)
    y_proba = model.predict_proba(X_test_scaled)[:, 1]
    acc     = accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred)
    auc     = roc_auc_score(y_test, y_proba)
    test_results[name] = {
        'accuracy': acc, 'auc': auc,
        'y_pred': y_pred, 'y_proba': y_proba
    }
    print(f"\n{'='*50}")
    print(f"  {name}")
    print(f"{'='*50}")
    print(f"  Test Accuracy:  {acc:.4f} ({acc*100:.2f}%)")
    print(f"  ROC-AUC Score:  {auc:.4f}")
    print(f"  Baseline:       {baseline_acc:.2%}")
    print(f"  Improvement:    +{(acc - baseline_acc)*100:.2f}%")
    print(f"\nClassification Report:")
    print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred,
          target_names=['Team B Won', 'Team A Won']))

Both models achieve identical test accuracy of 84.09% on the 44 held-out matches, a near-perfect translation of the 84.00% CV accuracy. This confirms that neither model overfit to the training data. Logistic Regression edges out SVM on ROC-AUC (0.913 vs 0.904), meaning it produces better-calibrated win probability estimates across all classification thresholds, not just the default 0.5 cutoff.

Looking at the classification report, Logistic Regression performs slightly better on the minority class (Team A Won): it achieves 76% recall versus SVM’s recall on Team A matches, correctly identifying more of the harder-to-predict upset wins. The macro-averaged F1-score of 0.83 for both models confirms balanced performance across both classes despite the 60/40 split in the training data.

The summary table confirms Logistic Regression as the preferred final model. Despite the identical test accuracy, its superior ROC-AUC of 0.913 versus 0.904 gives it a meaningful edge in win probability estimation. This is a more useful output than a binary prediction alone when analyzing competitive VCT match outcomes.

Confusion Matrices

The confusion matrix breaks down each model’s 44 test predictions into four categories: true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives. While overall accuracy treats all errors equally, the confusion matrix reveals where each model is making mistakes — whether it struggles more with correctly identifying Team A wins (the minority class) or Team B wins (the majority class).

Code

    cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, results['y_pred'])
    disp = ConfusionMatrixDisplay(confusion_matrix=cm,
                                   display_labels=['Team B Won', 'Team A Won'])
    disp.plot(ax=ax, colorbar=False, cmap='Blues')

plt.show()

Logistic Regression correctly predicts 24 of 27 Team B wins and 13 of 17 Team A wins, producing 3 false negatives (Team B wins predicted as Team A) and 4 false positives (Team A wins predicted as Team B). SVM shows a slightly different error distribution, correctly predicting 23 Team B wins and 14 Team A wins, with 4 false negatives and 3 false positives.

The two models essentially trade errors: Logistic Regression is marginally better at identifying Team B wins (the majority class), while SVM is marginally better at identifying Team A wins (the minority class). Neither pattern is clearly superior, which further supports using ROC-AUC as the tiebreaker, where Logistic Regression’s 0.913 gives it the edge.

ROC Curves

The ROC (Receiver Operating Characteristic) curve plots the True Positive Rate against the False Positive Rate across every possible classification threshold, rather than just the default 0.5 cutoff. The Area Under the Curve (AUC) summarizes this into a single number; a perfect classifier scores 1.0, while a random classifier that simply guesses scores 0.5. This makes ROC-AUC particularly informative for comparing models that tie on raw accuracy, as it evaluates the quality of the underlying probability estimates rather than just the final binary prediction.

Code 
# ROC Curves

colors = ['#2980B9', '#E74C3C']
for (name, results), color in zip(test_results.items(), colors):
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_test, results['y_proba'])
    ax.plot(fpr, tpr, color=color, linewidth=2.5,
            label=f"{name} (AUC = {results['auc']:.3f})")

ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], 'k--', linewidth=1, label='Random Classifier')
ax.fill_between([0, 1], [0, 1], alpha=0.05, color='gray')
ax.set_xlabel('False Positive Rate', fontsize=12)
ax.set_ylabel('True Positive Rate', fontsize=12)
ax.set_title('ROC Curves: Top 2 Models on Test Set',
             fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
ax.legend(fontsize=11)
ax.set_xlim([0, 1])
ax.set_ylim([0, 1.02])

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('eval_plot2_roc_curves.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

Logistic Regression’s curve (AUC = 0.913) sits consistently above SVM’s curve (AUC = 0.904) across the majority of the threshold range, particularly in the low false positive rate region on the left side of the plot (the most practically important region) where we want high confidence before calling a predicted winner. Both curves climb steeply away from the random classifier diagonal, confirming that the differential feature set provides strong discriminative power for predicting VCT match outcomes.

Based on the combined evidence from test accuracy, ROC-AUC, confusion matrix error patterns, and interpretability, Logistic Regression with Elastic Net regularization is selected as the final best model. Its linear structure allows direct coefficient interpretation of which performance differentials drive match outcomes, while its 0.913 AUC demonstrates reliable win probability calibration across all decision thresholds.

Testing the Model

Code 
# Team Stats Lookup + Name Aliases + Prediction Functions

# --- Build Team Stats Lookup ---
team_stats_lookup = {}

for _, row in match_df.iterrows():
    team_a = row['Team A']
    team_b = row['Team B']

    if team_a not in team_stats_lookup:
        team_stats_lookup[team_a] = []
    team_a_stats = {col: row[f'team_a_{col}'] for col in numeric_features}
    team_stats_lookup[team_a].append(team_a_stats)

    if team_b not in team_stats_lookup:
        team_stats_lookup[team_b] = []
    team_b_stats = {col: row[f'team_b_{col}'] for col in numeric_features}
    team_stats_lookup[team_b].append(team_b_stats)

# --- Average Each Team's Stats ---
team_avg_stats = {}
for team, stats_list in team_stats_lookup.items():
    stats_df_temp = pd.DataFrame(stats_list)
    team_avg_stats[team] = stats_df_temp.mean().to_dict()

# --- Apply Name Aliases ---
team_aliases = {
    'Mega Minors': 'NRG',
    'LEVIATÁN': 'LEV'
}

for old_name, new_name in team_aliases.items():
    if old_name in team_avg_stats:
        team_avg_stats[new_name] = team_avg_stats.pop(old_name)
        print(f"✅ Renamed '{old_name}' → '{new_name}' in team_avg_stats")
    if old_name in team_stats_lookup:
        team_stats_lookup[new_name] = team_stats_lookup.pop(old_name)
        print(f"✅ Renamed '{old_name}' → '{new_name}' in team_stats_lookup")
    mask_a = match_df['Team A'] == old_name
    mask_b = match_df['Team B'] == old_name
    match_df.loc[mask_a, 'Team A'] = new_name
    match_df.loc[mask_b, 'Team B'] = new_name

# --- Fit Scaler on Differential Features ---
diff_rows = []
for _, row in match_df.iterrows():
    diff = {col: row[f'team_a_{col}'] - row[f'team_b_{col}'] for col in numeric_features}
    diff_rows.append(diff)

diff_df = pd.DataFrame(diff_rows)
pred_scaler = StandardScaler()
pred_scaler.fit(diff_df)

# --- Base Prediction Function ---
def predict_matchup(team_1, team_2, verbose=True):
    if team_1 not in team_avg_stats:
        print(f"❌ '{team_1}' not found in dataset.")
        return None
    if team_2 not in team_avg_stats:
        print(f"❌ '{team_2}' not found in dataset.")
        return None

    stats_1 = team_avg_stats[team_1]
    stats_2 = team_avg_stats[team_2]

    diff = {col: stats_1[col] - stats_2[col] for col in numeric_features}
    X_input = pd.DataFrame([diff])
    X_input_scaled = pred_scaler.transform(X_input)

    prob = lr_grid.best_estimator_.predict_proba(X_input_scaled)[0]
    team_a_win_prob = prob[1]
    team_b_win_prob = prob[0]

    if verbose:
        winner = team_1 if team_a_win_prob >= 0.5 else team_2
        print("=" * 50)
        print(f"  ⚔️  {team_1}  vs  {team_2}")
        print("=" * 50)
        print(f"  🏆 Predicted Winner: {winner}")
        print(f"  {team_1:<25} {team_a_win_prob:.1%}")
        print(f"  {team_2:<25} {team_b_win_prob:.1%}")
        print("=" * 50)

    return {'team_a_win_prob': team_a_win_prob, 'team_b_win_prob': team_b_win_prob}

# --- Robust Prediction Function ---
def predict_matchup_robust(team_1, team_2):
    """
    Averages predictions from both team orderings to cancel out
    the positional bias caused by Team A/B naming convention imbalance.
    """
    r1 = predict_matchup(team_1, team_2, verbose=False)
    r2 = predict_matchup(team_2, team_1, verbose=False)

    if r1 is None or r2 is None:
        return

    avg_prob_1 = (r1['team_a_win_prob'] + r2['team_b_win_prob']) / 2
    avg_prob_2 = 1 - avg_prob_1
    winner = team_1 if avg_prob_1 >= 0.5 else team_2

    print("=" * 50)
    print(f"  ⚔️  {team_1}  vs  {team_2}  [ROBUST]")
    print("=" * 50)
    print(f"  🏆 Predicted Winner: {winner}")
    print(f"  {team_1:<25} {avg_prob_1:.1%}")
    print(f"  {team_2:<25} {avg_prob_2:.1%}")
    print("=" * 50)

# --- Run Prediction ---
predict_matchup_robust('100 Thieves', 'NRG')

Conclusion

This project set out to answer a core question: can aggregate team-level performance statistics from VCT match data reliably predict match outcomes? The answer, based on our modeling results, is a confident yes.

After engineering differential features across key performance metrics — Rating, KAST, Kills, Deaths, Assists, ACS, ADR, and First Kills — and evaluating two classification models via 5-fold stratified cross-validation, both Logistic Regression and SVM achieved 84.09% test accuracy, representing a +24.09 percentage point improvement over the 60% majority-class baseline. Logistic Regression was selected as the final best model based on its superior ROC-AUC of 0.913, reflecting better-calibrated probability estimates across all decision thresholds.

The strong performance of a linear model is itself informative: it suggests that match outcomes in VCT are not chaotic or unpredictable, but rather follow structured, statistically learnable patterns. Teams that outperform their opponents in Rating and KAST tend to win — and a simple linear boundary in feature space is sufficient to capture most of that signal.

Despite these results, the project has several notable limitations. The dataset consisted of only 144 matches from a single VCT season, which constrains both the statistical power and generalizability of the models. Match outcomes may also be influenced by factors not captured in aggregate statistics — such as map selection, agent composition, team economy, and in-game adaptations — all of which were unavailable in the dataset used here.

Additionally, because features were constructed as differentials between two teams, the model inherently requires both teams’ statistics to be observed before making a prediction. This limits the model’s utility for real-time or pre-match forecasting without additional data engineering.

Future work could expand this analysis in several meaningful ways:

  • Larger, multi-season datasets would improve model reliability and allow for temporal generalization testing across different VCT metas.
  • Map-level features (e.g., map win rates, agent picks by map) could capture strategic variance that aggregate stats obscure.
  • Tree-based ensemble models such as Random Forest or XGBoost could be explored to capture any non-linear interactions between features that the linear models may miss.
  • Time-series or rolling average features could be used to model team momentum and performance trends over a season rather than treating each match independently.

Overall, this project demonstrates that machine learning is a viable and effective tool for modeling competitive esports outcomes — and that even with limited data, meaningful predictive signal can be extracted from professional Valorant match statistics.
